source: Li, Fan, Cheng, Feizi, Zhou (2025) Schoenfeld's Anatomy of Mathematical Reasoning by Language Models (ThinkARM)
finding: Eight-category episode labels (Read, Analyze, Explore, Plan, Implement, Verify, Monitor, Answer) were applied by an LLM to 15 models. Annotation agrees well with a human gold set.
numbers: 410,991 sentences, 15 models, 100 Omni-MATH problems, 1,500 responses. Human-verified gold set 7,067 sentences from 99 problems. GPT-5 annotator 86.33% accuracy, kappa 82.85; GPT-4.1 86.10%; Gemini-2.5-Flash 82.90%; Gemini-2.5-Pro 80.89%.
limits: Automatic labels may add noise. Math only. Gold set is small next to the corpus. Page text read up to 100k of 114k characters.
agent_relevance: Episode labels from a strong LLM are reliable enough (about 86%) to code our own logs at scale. Use a guidebook prompt and spot-check with a gold subset.

source: Li et al. (2025) ThinkARM, Table 2 episode allocation
finding: Reasoning models spread tokens over Analyze, Explore and Verify. Standard models are mostly Implement.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1 (9,250 tokens avg): Implement 36.35%, Analyze 30.75%, Verify 10.16%, Explore 9.21%. QwQ-32B (12,504 tokens): Implement 35.71%, Analyze 24.53%. GPT-4o (690 tokens): Implement 40.77%, Explore 2.58%. Gemini-2.0-Flash: Implement 61.17%, Explore 0.97%. Phi-4: Implement 64.12%.
limits: Token shares are descriptive. They do not say which share is best.
agent_relevance: Gives a baseline episode profile. A scaffold run with Explore near 1% behaves like a non-reasoning model; one with Explore above about 9% behaves like R1.

source: Li et al. (2025) ThinkARM, Table 4 correctness case study
finding: Lasso logistic regression on episode transition features predicts correctness. Explore followed by Monitor or Analyze goes with success. A high Explore share and Explore going straight to Verify or Answer go with failure.
numbers: 500 stratified traces from 5 open-source reasoning models. Exp->Mon beta +0.41, Exp->Ana +0.31. Explore ratio beta -0.54, Exp->Ver -0.45, Exp->Ans -0.41. Imp->Read -0.32 in Table 4 but -0.33 in Table 7.
limits: Correlational. No AUC or held-out accuracy was extracted. Only 500 traces, 5 models. Small internal inconsistency between tables. Difficulty may drive both Explore share and failure.
agent_relevance: Core input for a coded impasse detector: many Explore sentences with no Monitor or Analyze pause after them is a failure sign. Needs our own validation.

source: Li et al. (2025) ThinkARM, Tables 5-6 efficiency methods
finding: Methods that shorten reasoning do not shorten it evenly. They cut Verify and Analyze steps selectively, and differ in how much of the baseline transition structure they keep.
numbers: Baseline R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B 9,897 tokens, Analyze 26.93%, Verify 11.43%. L1: 2,437 tokens, Analyze 18.34%, Verify 6.99%, max divergence 0.3762. ThinkPrune: 4,054 tokens, Verify 7.31%, divergence 0.1506. Arora and Zanette: 5,312 tokens, Verify 4.63%, divergence 0.1039.
limits: One small model (1.5B). No accuracy figure was pulled per method here. Divergence score is the authors' own measure.
agent_relevance: Budget cuts in our scaffold will silently remove verification. Keep a code-enforced verify step when trimming tokens (G2, G3).

source: Li et al. (2025) ThinkARM, Table 3 transition mutual information
finding: The most distinctive pattern of reasoning traces versus final answers and versus non-reasoning models is Explore-Monitor. Reasoning traces loop through Explore, Monitor, Verify; answers are feed-forward.
numbers: Exp-Mon mutual information 0.2862 (reasoning vs answer) and 0.2510 (reasoning vs non-reasoning). Traces normalized to 25 time bins.
limits: Distinguishes model types, not correct from incorrect.
agent_relevance: Monitor is the brief hesitation marker. Our detector can use Monitor presence as a cheap signal of live self-checking.

source: Li et al. (2025) Annotation of Schoenfeld-style episodes in LLM reasoning (arXiv 2509.14662)
finding: Seven sentence labels were hand-coded on DeepSeek-R1 answers to SAT maths. A guidebook helps LLM labelers more than examples. A fine-tuned or prompted GPT-4.1 reaches 0.805 sentence accuracy.
numbers: 1,385 SAT items, 19 skills, 38 R1 responses, 915 paragraphs, 3,087 sentences, 70/30 split. GPT-4.1 example+guidebook 0.805 acc, kappa 0.764. BERT 0.732, RoBERTa 0.730, SVM 0.704, MLP 0.684, KNN 0.587. Zero-shot sentence accuracy GPT-4.1 0.595 base, 0.676 guidebook, 0.681 ex+guide.
quote: the accuracy for automatic annotation is not very high, further efforts are needed
limits: Only 38 responses, one model, SAT maths. The 0.805 comes from the 30% test subset, small. Inter-rater agreement for humans was not given as a number. Paragraph level only 0.757 best.
agent_relevance: The 0.805 figure is the ceiling for cheap labelling on a tiny corpus. Zero-shot labels are weak (0.59-0.68), so a guidebook is needed.

source: Li et al. (2025) arXiv 2509.14662 confusion matrix
finding: Labelers confuse Analyze with Verify and Implement with Verify most. Verify is the hardest boundary.
numbers: GPT-4.1 diagonals: Read 11.3, Analyze 16.6, Plan 5.7, Implement 17.1, Explore 6.1, Verify 18.5, Monitor 5.2 (percent of all). Largest off-diagonal Analyze->Verify 4.8, Implement->Verify 3.2.
limits: Row-normalized percentages as read by a summarizer; exact cell layout not checked against the PDF.
agent_relevance: A detector should not rely on single-sentence Verify labels. Use code evidence (a check was actually run) rather than wording.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Thoughts Are All Over the Place: Underthinking of o1-like LLMs
finding: Incorrect answers use more tokens and many more thought switches than correct ones, and often drop a correct early thought without finishing it.
numbers: On average o1-like models use 225% more tokens in incorrect than correct answers, with 418% more thought switches. Test sets MATH500, GPQA Diamond, AIME2024 (plus 60 AIME 2022-23 items). Over 70% of incorrect responses contain at least one correct thought; in over 50% of them, more than 10% of thoughts are correct. Thought-correctness judge: 82.9% on correct, 81.8% on incorrect thoughts (90 instances, 35 correct and 55 incorrect thoughts).
limits: Switch detection relies on cue words like 'alternatively'. Two models only (QwQ-32B-Preview, R1). Correlational. Conventional models showed no such length gap.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for a wandering detector: count switch cues per token and flag unfinished promising branches. Rule: do not abandon a branch before a code-run check.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Underthinking: TIP decoding and best-of-N
finding: Penalizing switch tokens during decoding (TIP) raises accuracy without fine-tuning, and stacks with self-consistency and laconic decoding. Prompting alone changed little.
numbers: R1 on AIME2024: switch tokens fell from 13.8 to 5.7, average interval rose from 580.1 to 941.6 tokens. QwQ self-consistency Pass@4 43.7% to 51.4% with TIP. R1-Distill-Qwen-32B laconic Pass@4 74.4% to 78.0%, underthinking score 8.7 to 7.3. Grid: alpha in [3,5,10,20,30], beta in [300..700], tuned on AIME 2022-23.
limits: Needs logit access. Hyperparameters tuned on one model. Gain sizes are single-benchmark. Prompt-only guidance weak, so a scaffold cannot copy TIP with words.
agent_relevance: Suggests a hard code rule (minimum steps before switching strategy) beats a prompt that says 'stay on one approach'. Fits G1 and the program-decides rule.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=? On the Overthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: Reasoning models overthink easy problems: the first solution round is almost always already correct and later rounds add little.
numbers: 1,953% more tokens than conventional models on '2 plus 3', 13 solutions in one example. First round correct in over 92% of cases and uses under 60% of tokens (QwQ on ASDIV: 287 tokens, 38.7% of response). QwQ-32B-Preview gives 2-4 solution rounds in 76-80% of cases, R1 in 59-63%. Easier sets get more rounds (QwQ ASDIV 3.5 avg). Self-training cut tokens 48.6% on MATH500 with QwQ at preserved accuracy.
limits: Solutions split by Llama-3.3-70B. Accuracy preserved on MATH500; harder sets have smaller gains. Outcome efficiency metric counts only tokens to first correct answer.
agent_relevance: After the first verified correct answer, stop (adaptive stopping link). Later rounds mostly repeat the same strategy, so extra rounds should be code-gated.

source: Ma et al. (2025) Does Thinking More always Help? Understanding Test-Time Scaling in Reasoning Models
finding: Forced extra thinking ('Wait') helps at first, then hurts. A variance argument says the early gain may be noise. Parallel thinking within the same budget beats extended thinking.
numbers: R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B on GSM8K: 82.2% at 385 tokens, peak 87.3% near 1,100 tokens, 70.3% near 15,980 tokens. MATH500: 83.2% base, +1.5 at ~4,983 tokens, falls to 78.3% by ~16,109. Entropy 0.23 to 2.79 (GSM8K). Parallel thinking up to 22% above extended at 16K budget; GSM8K extended -11.8 vs parallel +10.1 points.
limits: Small distilled models (1.5B, 7B, 8B). Wait is forced by the experimenter, not model-chosen. Accepted NeurIPS 2025; the exact 20% or 22% figure differs by place in the paper.
agent_relevance: Do not force doubt on a schedule (G1 holds). Spend extra budget on independent attempts checked by code instead of longer chains.

source: Hassid et al. (2025) Don't Overthink It: Preferring Shorter Thinking Chains (arXiv 2505.17813)
finding: For the same question, shorter chains are more often correct than the longest sampled chain. Stopping parallel runs when the first m finish works.
numbers: Up to 34.5% more accurate than the longest chain. short-1@k matches or beats majority vote with up to 40% fewer thinking tokens. short-3@k beats majority voting at all budgets and cuts wall time up to 33%.
limits: Abstract page only was read; benchmarks and model list not seen. Within-question length effect, so not proof that length causes failure.
agent_relevance: Length itself is a usable failure signal within a problem. A cheap detector: a run that has gone far past its sibling attempts' length is likely wandering.

source: Feng et al. (2025) What Characterizes Effective Reasoning? Revisiting Length, Review, and Structure of CoT (Failed-Step Fraction)
finding: After controlling for question, longer chains and more review go with lower accuracy. The fraction of steps in failed exploratory branches (FSF) is the most consistent predictor across all models.
numbers: 10 models (Claude 3.7 Sonnet Thinking, Grok 3 mini, R1, Qwen3, gpt-oss and others). HARP 300 questions x 16 traces; GPQA-Diamond 198 questions; AIME 2025 30 problems x 64. Review ratio negative for most models; Claude 3.7 on math is positive. Correlations strongest on harder HARP levels 4-6. Review labels from Llama 4 Maverick with about 90% agreement on 30 traces.
limits: Numeric correlation coefficients appear only in figures, not text. Faithfulness of CoT not tested. Graph extraction by Claude. Qwen3 results maybe contaminated on HARP. First-failed-step depth showed little correlation.
agent_relevance: Best-supported trace-level failure signal: share of effort spent on branches that were later abandoned. Compute it from our own logs (operator attempts that failed checks).

source: Feng et al. (2025) Failed-Step Fraction interventions
finding: Selecting the trace with lowest FSF raises accuracy, and deleting failed branches from a wrong trace lets continuations succeed more often. Deleting beats summarizing the failed branch.
numbers: AIME 2025 top-1 of 64 by FSF: about +5 to +13% over random. Claude 3.7 self-selecting by FSF up to +12%. Editing 80 wrong R1 traces and 160 wrong gpt-oss-120B traces, 8 continuations each (11,520 total): R1 first failed branch removed 20.89% to 29.42% (+8.5), last branch 9.72% to 23.75% (+14.0); gpt-oss first 28.05% to 36.41% (+8.4), last 16.50% to 27.33% (+10.8). Summary variant: 28.14 / 22.57 / 29.51 / 25.22.
limits: Only incorrect HARP traces from two models. Edit experiment shows causal effect of context pruning, not of prior behaviour.
agent_relevance: Strong support for restarting from a clean context that omits dead ends (a reframe or restart operator) rather than keeping all failed text. Matches G2 and the not-add list on long histories.

source: Lu, Xu, Kankanhalli (2025) Reasoning LLMs are Wandering Solution Explorers
finding: Reasoning models explore without structure. Failures are invalid exploration (boundary violation, procedure omission, incorrect backtracking), redundant exploration, and evaluation errors. A wandering searcher's success falls exponentially with depth, and can hide as a plateau on easy items.
numbers: Six models: R1-Distill-Llama-8B, R1-Distill-Qwen-14B, QwQ-32B, R1, Claude Sonnet 3.7, o3. Open models run 10 times at temperature 0.6; API models run once. All six degrade with complexity; smaller models degrade faster, and even o3 and Sonnet 3.7 eventually do.
quote: performance could suddenly start to collapse when the problem complexity exceeds a certain threshold
limits: Position paper with formal argument plus case studies on computation tasks with programmatic ground truth, not maths olympiad problems. Under review. Per-failure-type rates not extracted.
agent_relevance: Benchmarks near ceiling can hide wandering. Our detector should test on depth-scaled tasks; a code-checkable audit of trace steps (rule by rule) is a model for our checks.

source: Chen and Wang (2026) A Comprehensive Anatomy of Human and DeepSeek-R1 LLM Mathematical Reasoning
finding: Successful traces use branching and backtracking in a moderate, steady way. Failed traces use too little or too much exploration. Reflection helps only inside deductive inference, not inside analysis loops. R1 loops through local checks without progress ('topological mimicry').
numbers: 30 AIME 2025 problems, 10,247 annotated steps, five categories: Analysis, Inference, Branch, Backtrace, Reflection. No per-category counts seen.
quote: reproducing the surface form of reasoning without its functional role
limits: Abstract page only. Single model. Does not use Schoenfeld labels. Preprint; no replication.
agent_relevance: Both too little and too much exploration fail, so the detector needs a band, not a one-sided threshold. Also flags reflection-in-analysis loops as a wild-goose-chase pattern.

source: Kang et al. (2025) First Try Matters: Revisiting the Role of Reflection in Reasoning Models
finding: Most reflection after a first answer just confirms it. Very few reflections fix a wrong answer. Training on more reflection mainly improves the first answer.
numbers: 8 models (7B to 685B), 5 math sets (AIME24, AIME25, AMC, OlympiadBench, Math500), 3,427 rollouts per model. Over 90% of reflections confirmatory; corrective (wrong to right) under 2%. Post-first-answer reflections use 16.8-47.8% of tokens for 1.4-3.5% accuracy. SFT cut-at-6 beat cut-at-1 by 4.05%, of which 3.75% was first-answer accuracy. RL: +4.6 vs +0.3 reflection (32B), +7.7 vs +0.1 (7B). Early stopping Qwen3-8B: 29.9% fewer tokens for 3.8-point drop; 24.5% fewer for 2.9. Candidate extraction rated correct 94%.
limits: Math only. The page held hidden encoded blocks that looked like instructions; ignored. Answer extraction by a model. Reflection counted only after a first candidate.
agent_relevance: The Verify episode is mostly wasted when it is self-judged. Real verification needs code output (G2, G3). Supports adaptive stopping after a code-checked answer.

source: Marjanovic et al. (2025) DeepSeek-R1 Thoughtology: Let's think about LLM Reasoning
finding: R1 chains follow problem definition, one long bloom cycle, then reconstruction cycles. Many later cycles re-check old assumptions (rumination) or abandon new ones. A sweet spot of length exists; longer than it hurts accuracy.
numbers: Bloom cycle is typically the longest. Long reconstruction cycle roughly every 5 cycles, with high variance. Rumination (5-gram repetition) rises with problem difficulty and is independent of total time. Correct thoughts are on average shorter than incorrect ones. Qwen3 and gpt-oss also show a sweet spot; gpt-oss has a different pattern. TMLR 2026, 135 pages.
quote: does not indicate faithful process monitoring
limits: Mostly one model, descriptive. No single accuracy effect size extracted. Rumination rate is a text-repetition proxy.
agent_relevance: Gives measurable rumination signals (n-gram repetition, revisiting an old assumption) usable as a cheap code detector. Also warns that expressed confidence is not monitoring.

source: Bogdan, Macar, Nanda, Conmy (2025) Thought Anchors: Which LLM Reasoning Steps Matter?
finding: By resampling after each sentence, planning and uncertainty-management sentences have more causal effect on the final answer than computation or fact retrieval sentences.
numbers: R1-Distill-Qwen-14B, 20 MATH problems solved 25-75% of the time, 40 responses, avg 144.2 sentences, 100 rollouts per sentence. Sentence shares: active computation 32.7%, fact retrieval 20.1%, plan generation 15.5%, uncertainty management 14.0%. Replicated on R1-Distill-Llama-8B (40 solutions). Probe macro-F1 0.71. Forced-answer importance points the other way (favors computation).
limits: Only 20 questions and one main model. Receiver-head scores confounded by position. Error correction not formally examined. Resampling expensive.
agent_relevance: Plan and uncertainty (Plan, Monitor-like) steps are leverage points. A detector should watch Plan sentences: that is where a wrong turn does damage.

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) Cognitive Behaviors that Enable Self-Improving Reasoners
finding: Whether a model improves under RL depends on whether it already shows verification, backtracking, subgoal setting and backward chaining. Priming with these behaviors, even with wrong solutions, equalizes Llama with Qwen.
numbers: Qwen-2.5-3B far exceeds Llama-3.2-3B under identical RL on Countdown. Priming with incorrect but well-structured solutions did about as well as correct ones. No exact accuracy figures on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract page only. Single task (Countdown) plus pretraining filter on OpenWebMath. Small 3B models. Training result, not a scaffold test.
agent_relevance: The behavior pattern matters more than answer correctness in the examples. Supports putting the four behaviors in the scaffold as explicit operators, but with a caveat that the evidence is on training.

source: Su, Healey, Nakov, Cardie (2025) Between Underthinking and Overthinking: An Empirical Study of Reasoning Length and Correctness
finding: Models overthink easy problems and underthink hard ones, so length is poorly calibrated to difficulty. Preference training for shorter answers cut length with acceptable accuracy.
numbers: No numbers on the abstract page. Authors: four; one version (30 April 2025).
limits: Abstract page only; numbers not read.
agent_relevance: A length budget should depend on difficulty. A fixed token cap fails both ways, so use the code-measured progress signal instead.

source: Artzt and Armour-Thomas (1992) Development of a cognitive-metacognitive framework for protocol analysis of mathematical problem solving in small groups
finding: Human episode coding was extended to read, understand, explore, analyze, plan, implement, verify, watch and listen for group work. Later studies reused the scheme with sixth graders and high-ability middle schoolers.
numbers: No reliability figure found. A secondary citation says reliability of parsed protocol analysis is substantial.
limits: Only a search listing was seen, not the paper. Reliability numbers not verified. Category set differs from Schoenfeld's six.
agent_relevance: Shows that episode schemes drift between studies (Understand vs Read, Watch and Listen). Our labels should be fixed in a guidebook and versioned.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Underthinking: Figure 3-4 difficulty dependence
finding: Thought switches rise with problem difficulty. On MATH500-Hard and GPQA, the stronger model (R1) had higher underthinking scores, while on AIME2024 it had lower. So underthinking does not track accuracy simply.
numbers: Models: QwQ-32B-Preview, R1-Preview, R1-671B. Example: one incorrect answer spent about 7,270 additional tokens without reaching the right answer.
limits: The relation between accuracy and underthinking score is mixed across datasets, which weakens a simple 'more switching is worse' reading.
agent_relevance: A switch-count threshold must be set per difficulty; use the within-problem comparison, not a global cut-off.

source: Ma et al. (2025) Does Thinking More always Help? entropy control
finding: A control shows the damage comes from overthinking and not from a longer context: appending the same reasoning step repeatedly did not raise entropy.
numbers: Entropy rose 0.23 to 2.79 on GSM8K (1.5B) and 0.02 to 0.12 then to 3.0 on MATH500 with more Wait steps. 1.5B, 7B and 8B distilled models; GSM-8K 1,320 items, MATH-500, AIME 2024 (30).
limits: Small models only. Rival explanation: the early gain is variance, not better reasoning, and that claim rests on the authors' probabilistic model.
agent_relevance: Rival explanations exist for the up-then-down curve; our own test should vary the number of forced re-checks on a fixed set.

source: Li et al. (2025) ThinkARM versus arXiv 2509.14662: cross-paper comparison of what was and was not tested
finding: The 2025 labelling paper (0.805 accuracy) did not test whether labels predict correctness. ThinkARM did, but with a Lasso on 500 traces and no stated held-out score. So no study yet shows that episode labels predict failure out of sample.
numbers: 2509.14662: 38 responses. ThinkARM: 500 traces, 5 models, 15-model corpus of 1,500 responses.
limits: This line is my reading of the two papers; the missing held-out test is an absence in the text I read, not proof it does not exist in the unread 14k characters.
agent_relevance: Open gap that our own logs can fill: train and test an impasse detector on episode features with held-out items.

source: Thoughtology and Failed-Step Fraction compared: do length-based predictors survive controls?
finding: Raw length correlates with failure partly because hard questions make longer chains. Only within-question comparisons remove this. FSF paper does this and still finds negative length effects, with exceptions (Claude 3.7 review ratio positive on math; GPQA mainly length).
numbers: HARP 300 questions x 16 traces; GPQA 198 questions. Within-question correlations, mixed-effects model agrees in sign.
limits: Coefficients not in text. Pooled results (such as Thoughtology Figure 4.3, correct thoughts shorter) are confounded by difficulty.
agent_relevance: Any detector must compare a run to siblings on the same problem. Global length thresholds will mislead.

source: Kang et al. (2025) First Try Matters: moderators
finding: Early stopping at a reflection-confidence point saves tokens with a small accuracy price, and the price grows with the savings.
numbers: Qwen3-8B: a 1-point accuracy drop allows 12.0% token cut; an 8.12-point drop allows 40.7%. Corrective reflections added at most 1.7 points between best and worst settings across varied response lengths (~1K tokens).
limits: One model for stopping. Candidate extraction was 94% correct, so about 6% noise in the labels.
agent_relevance: A tradeoff curve for the stopping rule: near 12% savings is almost free; beyond that it costs accuracy.

source: Lu et al. (2025) Wandering Explorers: formal argument on plateaus
finding: A model of a wandering agent doing depth-first search on a binary tree of depth d with m target leaves shows success falling exponentially with d, and a plateau above 0.995 when m>1 that can fool benchmark readers.
numbers: Figure 1 uses m>1 and a wandering parameter qw from 0.9 to 0.99. Plateau marked where success exceeds 0.995.
limits: A toy model, not fitted to real traces. The 'wandering' parameter is assumed.
agent_relevance: Easy benchmarks can look solved while the process is still unstructured. Evaluate our schema on tasks with deeper search, not only on ones that already pass.
